title: The Mother in a cat
hookLine: a temple priest at Dakshineswar feeds the Goddess's offering to a cat, because he sees her in it
carry: the goddess is in every creature
tomorrow: a singer on a train platform asks: how does the bird come and go?
last: THE GODDESS COMES HOME AS A DAUGHTER.

lines: A KALI TEMPLE ON THE RIVER.
cards: At Dakshineswar, a temple to Kali on the bank of the Ganges near Calcutta, food has been cooked and laid out for the Goddess, and the priest is supposed to present it to her image with the proper rites.
Instead, a cat wanders in, and the priest kneels and feeds the offering to the cat. The temple staff are horrified. Word reaches the owner of the temple.
The priest's explanation is simple: he saw the Mother in the cat. Today, that priest, met earlier on this path: Ramakrishna.

teach.b: In the stories his followers kept, Ramakrishna was a young priest who couldn't treat the image of Kali as a statue. He would cry to her like a child: Ma, are you real? Why won't you show yourself?
He was, by his own telling, close to despair, and the accounts say he reached for the sword that hung in the shrine.
In that moment, he said afterward, the walls, the doors, the temple all vanished, and he saw a shining ocean of light, wave after wave, rolling toward him.
It was the Mother. After that, the line between the image and the world got thin. That's the cat.
He wasn't careless with the rites. He'd started seeing the Goddess everywhere, so feeding a hungry cat was feeding her. Here the two streams meet in one person.

The accounts say he later took up Vaishnava devotion too, and for a time lived in the mood of Radha, longing for Krishna, the way Chaitanya's followers describe. A Shakta priest of Kali, weeping for Krishna.
That's the Shakta teaching at its plainest: the Goddess isn't only in the shrine; she is in every creature.

It's one reason many Hindu homes set out a little food for animals and birds before the family eats, one of the old daily offerings, bhuta yajna, the offering to living beings. Ramakrishna took it all the way.
Once he'd seen her, he found her in a cat.

how: Devotees visit the Kali temple at Dakshineswar, where Ramakrishna served as priest, and his sayings and stories are read and retold in Bengali homes and in the monasteries that carry his name.

games.q: what does “bengal's shakta and vaishnava streams” mean?
o: devotion to Kali and to Krishna, meeting in one Bengal life
the temple rites of Dakshineswar, kept in exact order
Bengal's rule that a priest serves only one form of God

games.q: the evening offering has been made at Nani's shrine, and the stray cat is at the back door, hungry. by Ramakrishna's story, how do you see it?
o: the same Mother you just offered to, hungry at the door.
a pest to keep away from holy food.
a test: food from the shrine must never go to an animal.
games.why: Ramakrishna fed the Mother's offering to a cat because he saw her in it. in the Shakta stream, she is in every creature.

practice: Rest your eyes on one ordinary thing near you, a plant, a cup, an animal, your own hand, and look at it as if it might be more than it seems, the way you'd look at someone you love who's asleep.

Then close your eyes and breathe; if you pray, greet God there, by whatever name you use. And if despair ever comes close for you, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams: Ramakrishna, a priest of Kali at Dakshineswar who saw the Mother in a cat, and also longed for Krishna like Radha. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Kali, the dark Mother, worshipped at the Dakshineswar temple where Ramakrishna served.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: the goddess is in every creature. A priest of Kali saw her in a hungry cat. Go gently.

sources.ref: Accounts of Ramakrishna by his disciples (e.g. the Kathamrita of Mahendranath Gupta, and Saradananda's Lilaprasanga): the vision of the Mother, the cat, the mood of Radha
Shatapatha Brahmana 11.5.6.1 and later household law: the five daily offerings, including bhuta yajna, the offering to living beings
